topics.title: Number lines
topics.intro: A number line is like a race track with numbers on it. Work out what each little step is worth, then count the steps.
topics.teach: Explain how you know what each step is worth on a number line from 0 to 100 with 10 steps.
topics.talk: Draw a number line from 0 to 20 on paper and ask {him} to mark where 13 goes.

topics.title: Fact families
topics.intro: If you know one fact, you know four! 7 + 3 = 10, so 3 + 7 = 10, 10 − 3 = 7 and 10 − 7 = 3.
topics.teach: Explain how 8 + 5 = 13 helps you work out 13 − 5.
topics.talk: Give {him} one fact and ask for the other three in the family.

topics.title: Doubling and halving
topics.intro: Double means two lots of the same. Half means two equal parts. They undo each other: double 6 is 12, half of 12 is 6.
topics.teach: Explain how to double 34 by splitting it into tens and ones.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to halve the number of grapes in a bowl, then check by doubling.

visual.caption: Two rows of 6: double 6 is 12. Split them into the two rows: half of 12 is 6.

topics.title: Turns and directions
topics.intro: A full turn takes you all the way round. A half turn faces you the opposite way. Clockwise is the way clock hands go: north, east, south, west.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between clockwise and anticlockwise.
topics.talk: Play robots: give {him} instructions like “quarter turn clockwise, 3 steps forward”.

visual.caption: Each arrow is a quarter turn clockwise. Two quarter turns make a half turn; four make a full turn.

topics.title: Reading scales
topics.intro: Rulers, jugs and thermometers all have scales. Not every mark has a number, so first work out what each mark is worth.
topics.teach: Explain how to read a jug when the marks go up in 100s but only some are numbered.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to read the temperature on a thermometer or the oven dial.

visual.caption: Only some marks have numbers. 10 steps from 0 to 100, so each step is worth 10.

topics.title: Grouping and sharing
topics.intro: Dividing can mean sharing equally, or making equal groups. Sometimes there are some left over: these are called the remainder.
topics.teach: Explain why 13 cars need 4 transporters if each carries 4.
topics.talk: Share some biscuits equally and ask {him} how many are left over.

visual.caption: 15 shared into 3 equal groups: 5 in each. 15 ÷ 3 = 5.
13 ÷ 4 = 3 remainder 1. The car left over needs a 4th transporter.

topics.title: Block charts and tables
topics.intro: A block chart (bar chart) shows numbers as tall bars. Always look at the scale on the side: it might go up in 2s!
topics.teach: Explain how to find the difference between the tallest and shortest bars.
topics.talk: Make a block chart of the family’s favourite fruits.

topics.title: Making amounts and change
topics.intro: There are lots of ways to make the same amount with coins. Finding change means counting on from what it costs to what you paid.
topics.teach: Explain two different ways to make 50p.
topics.talk: Play shops with real coins: price toys and give change.

topics.title: How long does it take?
topics.intro: Time passes in minutes and hours. To find how long something takes, count on from the start time to the finish time.
topics.teach: Explain how to work out when a 30-minute race finishes if it starts at quarter past 2.
topics.talk: Ask {him} how long until dinner, or how long the car journey took.

visual.caption: The race starts at quarter past 2…
…and finishes at quarter to 3. That is 30 minutes.

topics.title: More number facts
topics.intro: More facts to know by heart: days in a year, sides of shapes, and number words.
topics.teach: Explain how many days are in a year, and what a leap year is.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to spell a number word, like “twelve” or “forty”.

topics.title: Puzzles and proof
topics.intro: Greater depth means thinking hard: finding all the answers, spotting patterns and explaining why.
topics.teach: Explain how you know you have found ALL the ways.
topics.talk: Ask {him} a “what number am I?” puzzle at dinner.

topics.title: Multiplying and dividing by 10 and 100
topics.intro: Multiplying by 10 makes a number ten times bigger: the digits shift one place to the left. Dividing by 10 shifts them back.
topics.teach: Explain what happens to the digits of 7 when you multiply by 100.
topics.talk: Ask {him} how many pence are in £3, £5 and £10.

visual.caption: 34 × 10 = 340. Each digit moves one place to the left, and a 0 fills the ones.

topics.title: Perimeter
topics.intro: Perimeter is the distance all the way round the outside of a shape, like one lap of a race track.
topics.teach: Explain how to find the perimeter of a rectangle quickly.
topics.talk: Measure round a table or a book with a tape measure.

topics.title: Roman numerals
topics.intro: The Romans wrote numbers with letters: I = 1, V = 5, X = 10. You still see them on clocks and in film titles.
topics.teach: Explain why 4 is written IV, not IIII.
topics.talk: Find Roman numerals on a clock face, a building or a book.

items.prompt: How many days are in a year (not a leap year)?
items.explain: A year has 365 days. A leap year has 366: an extra day on 29 February.

items.prompt: How many weeks are in a year?
items.explain: 52 weeks, and one day more.

items.prompt: How many days are in a fortnight?
items.explain: A fortnight is two weeks: 2 × 7 = 14.

items.prompt: How many days are in September?
items.explain: “Thirty days has September, April, June and November…”

head: Days
Months
rows: January, March, May, July, August, October, December

items.prompt: Which month has 28 days (29 in a leap year)?
items.explain: February is the shortest month.

head: Days
Months
rows: January, March, May, July, August, October, December

items.prompt: How many grams are in 1 kilogram?
items.explain: Kilo means a thousand: 1 kg = 1000 g.

items.prompt: How many millilitres are in 1 litre?
items.explain: 1 litre = 1000 ml. A big bottle of pop is often 2 litres.

items.prompt: What number is “forty-seven” in digits?
items.explain: Forty = 4 tens, seven = 7 ones: 47.

items.prompt: What is the number word for 19?
items.explain: Nineteen keeps the “e” of nine: nine-teen.

items.prompt: What is the number word for 90?
items.explain: Ninety keeps the “e” of nine too: nine-ty.

items.prompt: How many sides does a quadrilateral have?
items.explain: Quad means four. Squares, rectangles and kites are all quadrilaterals.

items.prompt: How many edges does a cube have?
items.explain: 4 round the top, 4 round the bottom and 4 going up: 12.

visual.caption: 4 edges round the top, 4 round the bottom and 4 going up: 12.

items.prompt: What is the name of a 3D shape with a square base and triangle faces meeting at a point?
items.explain: Like the pyramids in Egypt!

items.prompt: Which is the smallest: 0, 10 or 1?
items.explain: Zero means none at all: it is smaller than every counting number.

items.prompt: How many different ways can you make 5 by adding two whole numbers (counting 0 + 5 and 5 + 0 as different)?

options.feedback: Did you remember 0 + 5 and 5 + 0? List them: 0+5, 1+4, 2+3, 3+2, 4+1, 5+0.
That is if you don’t count turnarounds (0 + 5, 1 + 4, 2 + 3). There are 6 when you list them all.

items.explain: Work systematically: 0 + 5, 1 + 4, 2 + 3, 3 + 2, 4 + 1, 5 + 0. Six ways. Going in order means you never miss one.

items.prompt: 4? + 23 = 68. What is the missing digit?
items.explain: The ones must make 8: ? + 3 = 8, so ? = 5. Check: 45 + 23 = 68.

items.prompt: I am a 2-digit number. My tens digit is 3. My ones digit is double my tens digit. What am I?

options.feedback: The ones digit is DOUBLE 3, which is 6.
The TENS digit is 3, so the number starts with 3.

items.explain: Tens = 3, ones = double 3 = 6. The number is 36.

items.prompt: 5, 10, 15, 20… Will 63 be in this pattern?

options.text: Yes: the pattern goes on forever
options.feedback: It goes on forever, but it only hits numbers ending in 0 or 5.
Backwards gets smaller, away from 63.

items.explain: Counting in 5s always lands on numbers ending in 5 or 0, so 63 is never reached.

options.feedback: 20 is what 15 + 5 makes. The other side needs to make 20 too: 12 + 8.

items.explain: The = sign means “is the same as”. 15 + 5 = 20, so 12 + ? = 20, and ? = 8.

items.prompt: Using the digits 4, 7 and 1 once each, what is the GREATEST 2-digit number you can make?

options.feedback: Put the biggest digit in the tens place: 74.
7 is right for tens, but 4 is bigger than 1 for the ones.

items.explain: Biggest digit in the tens (7), next biggest in the ones (4): 74.

items.prompt: There are some robots and some cats. Robots have 2 legs, cats have 4. There are 3 of them altogether, with 10 legs. How many are cats?

options.feedback: 3 cats would have 12 legs.

items.explain: Try it: 2 cats = 8 legs, 1 robot = 2 legs, total 10. Trial and improvement!

items.prompt: {hero} says: “If you double any number, the answer is always even.” Is that true for whole numbers?

options.text: No: double 3 is an odd number
options.feedback: Double 3 is 6, which is even!

options.text: Only when you double even numbers
options.feedback: Double 5 = 10, double 7 = 14: odd numbers doubled are even too.

items.explain: Doubling a number makes two equal groups, so it can always be put into pairs: even.

items.prompt: Two numbers add to 10 and one is 4 more than the other. What are they?

options.feedback: 6 is only 2 more than 4.
8 is 6 more than 2.

items.explain: 3 + 7 = 10, and 7 − 3 = 4. Try pairs that make 10 until the difference is 4.

items.prompt: Half of a number is 9. What is a quarter of the number?

options.feedback: 18 is the whole number. A quarter is half of 9.
A quarter is half of a half: half of 9 is 4 and a half.
That is half of 4 and a half. The whole is 18, so a quarter is 4 and a half.

items.explain: The whole is 18. A quarter is half of half: half of 9 = 4½. Greater depth answers can be halves!
